Real Hope, Real Change — for a fairer, greener Britain. I strongly support a bold, joined-up plan that puts people and planet first. We must accelerate the roll-out of renewable energy — more offshore and onshore wind, community solar and locally owned projects — so cheap, clean power is available to every town and village. That goes hand-in-hand with an immediate ban on new oil, gas and coal licences: we cannot keep opening the door for fossil fuel giants to profit while families struggle with their bills.

To cut emissions and household costs, I strongly support banning the sale of new petrol cars by 2030 and ensuring every new home is built with non-fossil-fuel heating, rooftop solar and high levels of insulation. Warm homes and affordable electric travel will save money and create skilled local jobs.

I also strongly support a carbon tax on fossil fuel sales, with revenues returned to the public as a dividend — making the transition fairer, not regressive. And because climate breakdown is global, I strongly support compensating people in other countries who are already suffering its effects.

This is about justice: public ownership of our energy, investing in communities, and sharing the benefits broadly. For the common good — fairer, greener communities and a secure future for everyone.

I strongly oppose this package of climate diktats. It’s a Westminster bubble fantasy dressed up as “saving the planet” but paid for by ordinary families, pensioners and small businesses.

First, ramping up wind farms and banning new oil and gas licences at the same time is economic self-harm. You can’t heroically plaster the countryside with turbines and then expect energy security – we’ll be left begging foreign suppliers while North Sea jobs vanish. Telling people they must stop buying petrol cars by 2030 and forcing every new home to use non-fossil heating, solar roofs and ultra-heavy insulation turns basic mobility and decent housing into luxury options, hikes upfront costs and wrecks household budgets.

A carbon tax with a promised “dividend” sounds neat on paper but just adds another layer of fiddly levies that businesses pass straight on to consumers. And while compassion overseas matters, turning our finite resources into a global compensation slush fund ignores the duty to prioritise British households who are being crushed by bills now.

This is not climate leadership — it’s an ideological crusade that says elites know best. Scrap these costly mandates, stop the war on drivers and farmers, and focus on affordable British energy and common-sense policies that protect livelihoods, not virtue-signal at voters’ expense. Scrap Net Zero to cut energy bills. Restoration, not ruin.

I broadly support this package — I like the focus on renewables, low-carbon homes, and stopping new fossil licences because they push us away from damaging industries — but my support is cautious rather than wholehearted. I’m most drawn to community-led renewables and mandatory energy-efficient homes since they feel tangible and locally beneficial, while I’m more wary of things like a fast 2030 petrol ban or a carbon fee without strong equity measures, and I’d want any international compensation to be transparent and well-targeted.

Real hope, real change — that’s what a fair, greener Britain looks like. I strongly support accelerating renewables like more offshore and onshore wind, because clean power is now the cheapest way to keep lights on, create good local jobs and cut bills. That goes hand in hand with banning new oil, gas and coal licences — we can’t afford to keep gambling with our future while profits flow to polluters.

I also strongly support ending the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. Electric transport is cleaner, cheaper to run and will make our streets quieter and healthier. New housing must be part of the solution: I strongly support mandating non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation standards on all new developments so homes are warm, cheap to run and carbon-free from day one.

A fair transition needs fair funding. I support a carbon fee‑and‑dividend: taxing fossil fuels and returning revenues to the public so working people aren’t hit while polluters finally pay. And because climate breakdown crosses borders, I strongly support compensating people in other countries suffering its worst impacts — justice means helping those least responsible for the crisis.

Together these policies form one coherent plan: reclaim energy for the common good, protect families from rising bills, and build resilient, thriving communities — For the Common Good, a Secure Future for Everyone.

Overall I like the direction of this package — it prioritises people and the planet — but my support is conditional on strong equity and local-consent measures. I slightly support accelerating renewables (I favour community‑led projects and careful siting to avoid ecological harm), slightly support banning new fossil licences if paired with a clear just‑transition for workers and regions, and slightly support a 2030 petrol‑car sales ban only if low‑income households get real help (subsidies, accessible used EVs, and much better public transport). I strongly oppose this entire eco-ideological package. It isn’t climate policy — it’s a costly, top-down experiment by the Westminster “Green Blob” that punishes ordinary people and hands the country to remote elites.

Rampant wind farms and blanket bans on new oil and gas licences will destroy our energy security and send bills skywards. Mandating non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and wall-thick insulation on every new home sounds nice in a Whitehall briefing, but it adds thousands to house prices and strangles small builders with red tape — while farmers watch productive land turned into solar graveyards.

A carbon tax with a so-called “dividend” is still a stealth price hike that makes energy, food and transport more expensive. And spending British taxpayers’ money to compensate people abroad before we’ve fixed our own nation’s priorities — that’s virtue-signalling, not common sense.

We should scrap these ideological diktats, unlock North Sea energy, cut green levies, and put affordable power back in the hands of hardworking families. Real patriotism is protecting jobs, scraps of the countryside and the family budget — not bankrupting them for a fashionable policy stunt. Scrap Net Zero to cut energy bills. Restoring Britain’s power and prosperity starts here.

I strongly oppose this entire eco-ideological package. It isn’t climate policy — it’s a costly, top-down experiment by the Westminster “Green Blob” that punishes ordinary people and hands the country to remote elites.

Rampant wind farms and blanket bans on new oil and gas licences will destroy our energy security and send bills skywards. Telling people they can’t buy a petrol car after 2030, imposing ULEZ-style restrictions by stealth, and forcing costly electric conversions is a regressive assault on drivers and rural communities who rely on cars for work and family life. Mandating non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and wall-thick insulation on every new home sounds nice in a Whitehall briefing, but it adds thousands to house prices and strangles small builders with red tape — while farmers watch productive land turned into solar graveyards.

A carbon tax with a so-called “dividend” is still a stealth price hike that makes energy, food and transport more expensive. And spending British taxpayers’ money to compensate people abroad before we’ve fixed our own nation’s priorities — that’s virtue-signalling, not common sense.

We should scrap these ideological diktats, unlock North Sea energy, cut green levies, and put affordable power back in the hands of hardworking families. Real patriotism is protecting jobs, scraps of the countryside and the family budget — not bankrupting them for a fashionable policy stunt. Scrap Net Zero to cut energy bills. Restoring Britain’s power and prosperity starts here.

I oppose this whole package outright. It’s a Westminster green crusade — expensive, ideological and out of touch with ordinary people who just want to heat their homes and keep food on the table.

First, cramming the countryside and coasts with more wind parks and banning new oil and gas licences is economic vandalism. We should be boosting North Sea production to keep bills down and secure jobs, not strangling domestic energy and importing more expensive, unreliable power. Forcing an earlier ban on petrol cars by 2030 and mandating electric-ready homes with rooftop solar, exotic heating systems and extra insulation will shovel massive upfront costs onto families, pensioners and small businesses already crushed by high bills. They won’t be able to afford the switch, and supply chains will groan.

A carbon tax, even with a dividend, still props up the same elite narrative: make energy dearer to engineer behaviour. Passing more money around won’t fix the damage to wages and industry. And while compassion overseas matters, turning domestic policy into a global compensation slush fund while our own communities suffer is the wrong priority.

This is net zero by diktat — Net Zero is Net Poverty. Scrap these measures, remove green levies, expand sensible domestic production and put working British families first. Restore Britain’s power and prosperity.

Real Hope, Real Change — For the Common Good.

I strongly support a joined-up climate platform that puts people and communities first. We must accelerate renewable energy now — more offshore and onshore wind, community-owned solar and storage — so power is cheap, local and democratically run instead of lining corporate pockets. That means banning new oil, gas and coal licences: fossil fuels are a dead end that keep bills high and the planet heating. To drive the transition, we should ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030, backed by investment in public transport and charging for everyone, not just the wealthy.

Homes are where people feel the benefits: I strongly support mandating non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation in all new developments so families stay warm, cut bills and cut emissions. To make polluters pay, I support a carbon fee-and-dividend — a fair carbon tax on fossil fuels with revenues returned to households, protecting low-income families while speeding the shift to clean energy. And because Britain has a responsibility to the global community, I support compensating people in other countries suffering climate impacts, through finance and technology-sharing.

This is a plan that tackles the cost-of-living and the climate crisis together: public ownership, wealth redirected to communities, and a secure future for everyone. Fairer, Greener Communities.

Real hope, real change — that's what a fairer, greener Britain looks like in practice. I strongly support a bold, joined-up set of policies: accelerate renewable energy now — more onshore and offshore wind parks — and immediately stop issuing new oil, gas and coal licences. Renewable power is cheaper and cleaner, and ending new fossil extraction stops the cycle that keeps bills and emissions high.

I also strongly support banning the sale of new petrol cars by 2030 and making every new housing development non-fossil-fuelled, with rooftop solar and high levels of insulation. Together these measures cut household bills, create local jobs in retrofit and renewables, and give renters and owners warm, healthy homes.

To make the transition fair, I back a carbon fee-and-dividend: tax fossil fuel sales and return revenue to people, protecting low-income households while shifting costs onto polluters. And because climate breakdown is global and we have a responsibility to act, I support compensating communities abroad suffering from climate impacts — solidarity that builds trust and justice.

This package is coherent: public investment in renewables, strong standards for homes and transport, polluter pays, and international solidarity. It’s about putting people and planet before profit — fairer, greener communities and a secure future for everyone.

I strongly oppose this entire package of climate prescriptions. It’s not a coherent plan — it’s an ideological assault on ordinary people dressed up as “green” virtue-signalling. Forcing through an accelerated roll-out of wind farms and slapping bans on new oil, gas and coal licences will hollow out our energy security and hike bills, especially for the North Sea workforce and the communities that depend on it. Banning petrol cars by 2030 and mandating electric-ready homes with rooftop solar, exotic heating systems and top-tier insulation sounds fine in Westminster seminars, but in reality it shoves huge upfront costs onto hard-working families, small businesses and first-time buyers who can’t afford to retrofit or replace their cars on command.

A carbon tax with a rebate sounds clever on paper, but it just institutionalises a new hidden tax on heating and transport that households invariably feel long before any modest dividend arrives. Compensating other countries might win applause at UN conferences, but it’s taxpayers here who are being asked to foot the bill while our own infrastructure and living standards suffer.

This package treats Britain as a moral exhibit for global elites rather than a nation that must protect jobs, keep bills down and preserve practical freedoms like driving. Scrap the diktat — prioritise domestic energy production, strip green levies from bills and put common sense back at the heart of policy. Net Zero is net poverty; we should be restoring Britain’s power and prosperity instead.

I strongly oppose this whole package of climate diktats because it’s not about saving the planet — it’s about imposing an expensive, out-of-touch ideology on ordinary people who are already struggling. Ramming through rushed offshore and onshore wind parks and banning new oil, gas and coal licences will hollow out our energy security, hand control to green bureaucrats and foreign supply chains, and jack up bills for families and firms. Telling people they must buy electric cars by 2030 and outlawing petrol sales ignores reality: many hard-working Brits — rural folk, small businesses, and older drivers — rely on affordable, practical vehicles. Forcing every new home to have non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and extreme insulation loads builders with costs that get passed on to buyers and renters. Slapping a carbon tax on fuels, even with a supposed “dividend”, is just another stealth tax that hits the poorest hardest and stokes inflation. And spending British money to compensate people overseas takes cash away from our NHS, schools and farmers who feed us. In short: this package is Net Zero by command, not common sense. We should scrap these costly mandates, lift green levies, back British energy production and protect jobs — put power back in the hands of people, not the Green Blob.

Real hope, real change — that’s the kind of joined-up plan we need to protect people and planet. I strongly support a swift roll‑out of renewable energy, from offshore wind to community solar, because clean power is now the cheapest option and a huge job creator for towns that have been left behind. That’s why I also strongly support a ban on new oil, gas and coal licences: we cannot keep opening the door to the very industries that profit while pushing us toward catastrophe.

To make the transition fair and fast, I strongly support banning the sale of new petrol cars by 2030, paired with free or affordable public transport for young people and investment in charging infrastructure. I strongly support making all new homes zero‑carbon at the point they’re built — non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and top‑grade insulation — so families aren’t locked into high bills and we cut emissions from the start.

A fair carbon tax (fee and dividend) is something I strongly support: put a price on pollution, return the revenues to the public, and protect low‑income households while accelerating the low‑carbon shift. And because climate breakdown is already hitting vulnerable communities abroad, I strongly support compensating people in other countries who are impacted by our historic emissions.

I broadly support speeding up renewables — more offshore and onshore wind makes sense to cut bills and create jobs, as long as siting and community consent are handled properly. I’m generally in favour of banning new fossil licences, but I’d want a phased approach with clear just‑transition funding for affected workers and regions rather than a sudden cutoff. I back a 2030 end to new petrol sales in principle, though only if coupled with big investments in charging, support for rural drivers and grants so poorer families aren’t left behind. Requiring new homes to have non‑fossil heating, solar and good insulation is sensible and long‑term cost‑saving; again, support for small builders and protections for affordability are important. A carbon fee‑and‑dividend appeals to me as a fair way to price emissions, provided the design is transparent and genuinely redistributive to protect low‑income households. I’m sympathetic to compensating climate‑impacted people abroad on moral grounds, but such payments need strict oversight and measurable outcomes to ensure the money helps those who need it.

Real hope, real change — that’s the kind of plan we need to protect families and communities while confronting the climate emergency head-on. I strongly support accelerating renewable energy right now: more offshore and onshore wind and rooftop solar mean cheaper, cleaner power owned in the public interest so profits stay local. That goes hand-in-hand with a firm ban on new oil, gas and coal licences — we cannot keep signing new contracts with the forces that are driving up bills and wrecking our planet.

To speed the shift off fossil fuels, I strongly support banning the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2030, paired with free or affordable public transport for young people and safe, green streets. I strongly support mandating that all new homes have non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and high levels of insulation — insulation is the single biggest bill-buster and makes homes healthier.

I support a fair carbon fee-and-dividend: tax fossil fuel sales and return the revenue to people so households — not polluters — benefit. And because climate harm is global, I support compensating communities abroad who are already paying the price for our emissions.

Together these policies form one coherent platform: public ownership, bold standards, and fair returns to people — a secure future for everyone, for the common good.

I strongly oppose this whole package of Net Zero dogma dressed up as “climate policy.” Forcing through a rapid roll-out of wind farms, banning new oil and gas licences, outlawing petrol cars by 2030, mandating non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and super‑insulation on every new home, slapping a carbon tax on fuels and routing payouts abroad — it’s all the same top‑down project from the Westminster/Green Blob elite that punishes ordinary people while doing nothing for energy security.

This agenda will push up bills and taxes, strip energy jobs from the communities that built this country, and make farmers watch productive land vanish under turbines and panels. Banning licences and rushing petrol bans means higher transport and heating costs for families who can least afford it. Mandates on new homes add thousands to build costs, hitting first‑time buyers and small builders. A carbon tax is just another regressive squeeze, even with a “dividend” gimmick that won’t keep pace with rising prices. And spending scarce pounds compensating people abroad while British households freeze is not charity — it’s political theatre.

We need common‑sense solutions: scrap the Net Zero crusade, lift green levies, back domestic energy production in the North Sea, and protect drivers, farmers and small businesses. Restore Britain’s power and prosperity — not poverty by ideology.
